open-question.question: The recorded decisions fix the one-liner word for word but describe the new bold README tagline only by intent (it keeps the cairn trail-marker image and says the path is marked before the walk, so the walk can be handed off, without repeating the one-liner). What is the exact wording of the tagline that replaces "Mark the path from idea to shipped."?
open-question.recommendation: It states both halves of the recorded intent inside the trail image, the path marked before the walk and the walk handed off, in one short line that keeps the familiar "Mark the path" opening. Its single echo of the one-liner, the handoff verb, is the image paired with its plain statement rather than a repeat, while the other wordings repeat "your agent", open two lines in a row with "Cairn", leave the order or the agents unsaid, or leave the project's most visible line to be chosen during an unattended completion.
open-question.alternative: The tagline is one imperative sentence addressed to the reader. It drops the idea-to-shipped span and states the order directly, with the literal handoff verb: "Mark the path first, then hand off the walk." The walker is not named. It is short and states both parts of the recorded intent, the path marked before the walk and the walk handed off, in the trail image. The opening "Mark the path" keeps continuity with the current line. The idea-to-shipped span is lost from the first screen. "Hand off" echoes the one-liner's verb directly below it. The imperative form carries the same open reading of the product-noun decision as any reader-addressed tagline.

The tagline is two imperative sentences addressed to the reader. The first is the current line kept word for word, and the second adds the handoff with the literal verb: "Mark the path from idea to shipped. Then hand off the walk." The walker is not named. The first half is the existing line unchanged, so returning visitors still recognise it. It also keeps the idea-to-shipped span on the first screen, which the one-liner no longer carries now that milestones have left it. It is the longest option. "From idea to shipped" describes the whole arc rather than the split between before and after the walk, so the decide-upfront point rests on the second sentence alone. "Hand off" echoes the one-liner's "hand long-running execution". The imperative also leaves the reader as the subject, which conflicts with the product-noun decision if that decision's rule that "each pitch sentence makes Cairn the subject" is read to cover the tagline.

The tagline is one imperative sentence addressed to the reader with the span dropped. The handoff is stated only through the image, and the walker is named as the agent: "Mark the path, and let your agent walk it." It says who takes over in plain words while staying inside the trail image, with no handoff verb. A first-time reader connects the image to agents before reaching the one-liner. "Your agent" repeats the one-liner's "to your agent" on the very next line, against the recorded intent that the two lines not say the same thing twice. "Before the walk" is only implied by the word order. The imperative form carries the same open reading of the product-noun decision.

The tagline is one declarative sentence with Cairn as its subject, close to the recorded intent's own wording, with the span dropped and the literal handoff verb in the passive: "Cairn marks the path before the walk, so the walk can be handed off." The walker is not named. It follows the product-noun decision literally, since Cairn is the subject of what it does. It also states the recorded intent almost word for word, so nothing in it needs interpreting against the decision. The tagline and the one-liner would be two sentences in a row that both open with "Cairn" and share the same "so you can hand off" shape, which works against wording the two together so they do not say the same thing twice. The repeated "the walk" also makes it heavier than a bold tagline usually is.

The tagline is one impersonal declarative sentence with no reader or product as subject and the span dropped. It names the trail markers themselves rather than "mark the path", and states the handoff only through the image, leaving the walker unnamed: "Once the cairns are up, anyone can walk the trail." It is the purest form of the trail-marker image. It shares no word with the one-liner, and it echoes the product name directly under the "# Cairn" title. It sidesteps both the reader-as-subject and the double-"Cairn" problem. "Anyone" does not point at agents, and "trail" and "cairns" replace the familiar "Mark the path" phrase, so the line is the most abstract option and depends entirely on the one-liner to say what it means. The title word appears again as a common noun one line below the title.

The tagline is one short imperative sentence addressed to the reader with the span dropped. The handoff is stated as the reader leaving rather than someone else walking, and the walker is not named: "Mark the path, then walk away." It is the shortest and most quotable option, and it shares no words with the one-liner. It answers directly the new first paragraph of "Why Cairn?", which is built on the problem that "you cannot walk away". Inside the image, walking away sounds like abandoning the path rather than handing it to another walker, so it can read as careless rather than confident. That the walk still happens without the reader is left to the one-liner. The imperative form carries the same open reading of the product-noun decision.

No exact wording is recorded now. The README tagline decision stays at the level of intent, like the recorded decisions for "Why Cairn?", the "CLAUDE.md" opening, and the design-principle glosses, and whoever completes the README first-screen task writes the tagline next to the fixed one-liner within that intent. It matches how the milestone already records most prose surfaces, and it lets the tagline be written while the actual first screen, with the new diagram and one-liner, is in front of the writer. The milestone's own claim is that important questions are decided before execution, yet the most visible line on the project would be chosen during an unattended completion with no recorded decision behind it. The wording would also come out of no reviewed option set, so it could repeat the one-liner after all.
